Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. ### Commit-body form

The specimen is [commit-model.md](commit-model.md). A commit body is the [Problem-first
shape](#problem-first-shape) with one addition: a body whose
problem has several sub-problems arranges them by a fixed recursion, so a reader knows what any
bullet is from its marker and its depth. The earlier statement, "a problem statement then a solution
statement, both broad", left that arrangement to taste, and taste converged slowly and separately.

- **An intro paragraph states the general problem**, and defines any word the title assumes. It is
  mandatory. [Prose form](#prose-form) wants it regardless, and a body opening on a bullet is a body
  a `--body` flag can mistake for an option. The problem is *this commit's*, never the cycle's: the
  cycle's problem lives in the In Progress block, and a body whose problems outnumber what the diff
  resolves is describing something larger than the commit.
- **`*` bullets are the problem's facets**: sub-problems that decompose the intro's general problem,
  not a grab-bag of unrelated fixes. A body reaching for unrelated problem bullets is usually asking
  to be more than one commit.
- **`-` bullets are solutions**, and every `-` sits under a `*`, solving that facet. A `-` with no
  `*` above it reads as a solution to nothing, so there are no top-level solutions: a solution that
  retires every facet at once is written under each, or the facets are one.
- **One facet is the trivial commit**: the intro, one `*`, one or more `-` under it. Not a second
  form, the general form at its smallest.

  its body is the intro paragraph alone, naming the cycle by its title and pointing at its record,
  the In Progress block. No `*`, no `-`.

pairing is what a reader counts on: the `-` answers the `*` above it, with no rule to consult. The

read as plain text, in `jj log` and in terminals, where the markers survive, and if a renderer ever
flattens them the indentation still carries the structure. So the mixed markers are deliberate, and
a linter's consistent-marker rule is wrong to normalize them.

In this repo's vocabulary, "Land" is a defined term, not the general verb. AGENTS.md > Terminology:

> Land: the sequence that makes a cycle permanent, on the user's go at the close-out. Before it the cycle is a draft on its bookmark, after it the commits are permanent.

And Close-out step 6 spells the sequence out: restore the plain artifact name, reshape per the chosen close-out shape (trapezoid by default), fast-forward `main`, install the artifact, delete the bookmark locally and remotely.

So it maps onto your description like this:

- Your "lands on a branch, submitted for review": here that is the cycle running on its bookmark, reviewed rung by rung at each push (the work review and description review in the per-rung flow). There is no separate submit-for-review step, since author and repo owner are the same person and the review happens per rung.
- Your "inclusion into a pre-release branch, maybe someday a release branch": here there is only `main`. Land merges the bookmark's ladder onto `main` directly, no intermediate branch. The dual-repo model has no pre-release stage today.

The capitalized proper noun is deliberate in the agent-files: it names that specific sequence (step 6), so "at Land" means "at close-out step 6", the way "Trapezoid" names a specific merge shape. In a commit body, though, the proper noun reads oddly, as you say, because the body is read outside the agent-files. The body could say "The close-out ends when the cycle lands on `main`" instead, which is the same fact in plain words.

The plain version: "Land" here is the repo's name for the last close-out step, merging the finished cycle onto `main` and cleaning up. There is no review branch or pre-release branch in this model, the bookmark goes straight to `main` once you say go.

Assessment, since this is a convention question rather than the rung in flight.

Where the agent-files assume author = repo owner, as far as I can find:

- Land (Close-out step 6): the agent fast-forwards `main` and deletes the bookmark. That only works when the user controls `main`.
- Cycles run on a bookmark: "`main` advances only when the finished cycle lands on it." Same assumption, stated as a rule.
- Close-out shapes: trapezoid merge vs keep separate is a choice the cycle makes, but on a foreign repo the owner's merge policy makes it (squash-merge, rebase, merge commit).

What does not assume it: approval per push, the per-rung flow, the cycle-record, the bookmark per cycle. Those work the same whether the bookmark ends in a local merge or a pull request. And jj.md already has "Long-lived bookmarks: merge-only by default, deletable once merged", which is most of the foreign-repo case: the bookmark outlives the close-out until someone else merges it.

So generalizing is cheap in text: Land becomes "the bookmark is handed to the trunk's owner", with two endings, the owner is the user (today's sequence, merge and clean up) or the owner is someone else (push the bookmark, open the review request, and the cycle closes as a `## Waiting` entry on the merge, the bookmark deleted once merged). Everything else stays.

On necessity: every member today is wink-owned, so nothing is broken. It is also the kind of assumption that goes unnoticed until the first foreign repo, and then it is Land that has to change while a cycle is open. I would write the generalization down now, but as its own thing, not into this rung, which is already two subjects wide.

Per Unplanned work, your pick: a rung inserted into this cycle (it is convention work, so it fits the cycle's subject), or a `## Todo` entry for a later cycle. My recommendation is the entry, since you are not sure it is needed, and the entry costs nothing until it is.

For the body in flight, I would keep the wording as is except one line, "The close-out ends at Land" becomes "The close-out ends when the cycle lands", which is true under either model.

The plain version: the rules assume you own `main`. Only the last step, merging and cleanup, actually depends on that, and it could be written as "hand the bookmark to whoever owns the trunk" without touching anything else. Not needed today, worth a Todo entry, and this rung's body just needs "at Land" softened to "when the cycle lands".
